title: Tex's jazz-leaning radio show and early black radio
summary: Tex describes his theme song, playing Woody Herman, Ellington, Basie and Gillespie, his patter, and the start of black radio and payola.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Well, well, did you, I know you probably did, and there's a whole article in the Jazz Archivist. Yeah. And we're talking about New Orleans in the 60s, and they're talking about, a lot of it about the modern jazz scene. Did you follow the pop, the bebop scene in New Orleans?

Well, you know, really, if you think about it, uh, if you think about it, when I first went on the end, uh, my, uh, theme song was Blue Flame by Woody Herman. And a lot of people say, well, here's a black dance jockey playing black, white music, but hell, I was a lover of the music that Woody Herman played, and Stan Kenton played, and the rest of the guys, you know, I played white, I played Duke Ellington, I played Count, I played Dizzy Gillespie, I played it all. In fact, I was more of a jazz, a jazz disc jockey, much more so than a rock and roll, a pop type of disc jockey. Occasionally I would play, uh, like in the evening when, uh, George Augustine would get off there, you know, he was a disc jockey at one time, working at Old Governor Marwai. So he got off one eating right behind him, I said that the cool would be, when he'd get ready to dish out the good old under plunder, Mr. Cool would be around, sit down at the table if you're able with your family, and let us not only surprise you, but let you get this musical exercise, and the sound, that's in the scene, and it's very clean if you dig what I mean. And then I would segue into something very soft, like, uh, Body and Soul by Count Basie, or something with jazz overtones like that. Occasionally I'd come back with a Billy Eckstein, you know, thing, you know. So I was doing two different kinds of programs. I wouldn't say a hard jazz program, but then again, I would probably do the, uh, uh, occasionally I would get into the soft blues. I wouldn't get into the hard stuff. I would get sometimes into the Dino Washington stuff every now and then, you know. And it all depends on the mood, how it would hit me. Uh, and sometimes the weather had a heck of a lot to do with it, you know. I never know what the heck I'm on. And then, in those days, now you gotta remember, we talk about in the, in the fifties now. See, when we blacked disc jockeys at that time, this was a little bit before the thing called payola. You heard it talk about payola. All right. Uh, when black artists started getting popular, here's where the payola thing started coming in from, uh, uh, major cities. See, the first major so-called radio station that went on the air was WDIA up in Memphis, Tennessee, with Nat Williams in that country. That's where Dr. Webb B. B. King got his start playing up and around Memphis after leaving Mississippi. Of course, of course, he's one of my very, very dear friends and one of my fraternity brothers. They were both friends on Macy's B. B. King. In fact, he gifted me with one of his gold hems. I don't have it today, but I wear it every now and then. I think you've seen it. Well, anyway, so, uh, here we go from rock into the blues into the jazz kind of thing. But I started playing the jazz music because I thought there was, uh, there was a market for it. But even though rock and roll and Dr. Daddy or Ernie, they got more mail, they probably got three to four times more mail than I had because I was mostly trying to dignify the, the new, the new modern jazz. Occasionally I played a Louis Armstrong every now and then. But I was looking at, uh, uh, the, the, the thing from the Glenn Miller era to the Count Basie era, moving into another era, uh, where we had new, not new musicians, but these guys had, had, had been on the scene for quite a while. And, uh, you know, uh, you start talking about, uh, like I said, I mentioned, Count Basie there. And you start talking about, uh, trying to think another guy that I used to like to play.
